title: Short Stuff: iSmell
summary: Short Stuff episode on the iSmell, a 2000-era USB desktop peripheral that released scents matching websites being viewed. The hosts cover the feed consolidation announcement, the origins of the company DigitSense (founders Joel Bellensen and Dexter Smith, roughly twenty million dollars in venture capital), the idea of digitizing scent using a palette of 128 primary odorants, how the device heated odorants and blew air across them, its debut at the 2001 CES, its commercial failure, and its inclusion on PC World's 2006 list of worst tech products.

segments.title: Opening banter and feed announcement
segments.summary: The hosts joke about being short, announce that Short Stuff episodes will move from the standalone feed into the main Stuff You Should Know feed, and introduce the iSmell topic as a live-event tidbit.

segments.title: What the iSmell was
segments.summary: The iSmell was a desktop USB peripheral that released scents matching the websites a user browsed. The hosts note its Apple-like naming and say the device was either ahead of its time or poorly conceived from the start.

segments.title: DigitSense founders and the dot com era
segments.summary: The hosts describe the dot com boom and the founders Joel Bellensen and Dexter Smith, who formed DigitSense with about twenty million dollars in venture capital after earlier genetics database software work. The story goes that they got the idea in Miami Beach from perfume smells in the air.

segments.title: Digitizing scent and the odorant palette
segments.summary: The founders built a digital database of scent codes, linking odorant molecules to olfactory receptors. They reduced the problem to a palette of 128 primary odorants that could be combined into many smells.

segments.title: How the iSmell worked and why it failed
segments.summary: The device heated odorant cartridges and blew air across them to waft scents, and websites could send scent instructions via pixels. Despite working technically and being cheap to run, it was never consumer tested. It debuted at CES 2001, nobody wanted it, no units sold, and it was named to PC World's 2006 list of worst tech products.
topics: PC World worst tech products list

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: The hosts close the episode and invite listeners to contact the show through its website, social links, and email.
